title: Partita No. 2 in D minor for solo violin
hook: Four short dances, then the Chaconne, a quarter of an hour for one violin built on a four-bar phrase.

painting.title: Vanitas Still Life with Self-Portrait
painting.pairingNote: A violin and its bow lie beside a skull, an overturned glass and an open pocket watch, a meditation on time and loss; some scholars hear the Chaconne as Bach’s own memorial.

facts: Bach wrote out the six *Sei Solo a Violino senza Basso accompagnato*, “six solos for violin without bass accompaniment”, in a fair copy dated 1720, at Köthen, where he was music director to Prince Leopold. Three are sonatas; three, including this one, are partitas, Bach’s word for a [[suite|suite]] of dances.

The partita has four dances, [[allemande|allemande]], [[courante|courante]] (here Italian *Corrente*), [[sarabande|sarabande]] and [[gigue|gigue]] (*Giga*), followed by a [[chaconne|chaconne]] (*Ciaccona*), a long chain of [[variation|variation]]s on a four-bar phrase. The Chaconne lasts about as long as the four dances together.

A violin plays one line at a time, but Bach asks it for chords of three and four notes and for several voices at once. Brahms, who arranged the Chaconne for piano left hand, wrote to Clara Schumann that in it Bach puts on one stave “a whole world of the deepest thoughts and most powerful feelings”.

In the summer of 1720, while Bach was away with the prince at the spa of Carlsbad, his first wife, Maria Barbara, died suddenly. The musicologist Helga Thoene has argued that the Chaconne is a memorial to her. It is a theory, and a disputed one.
bigPicture.inOneLine: four dances in D minor (I–IV), then a set of variations that passes from minor to major and back (V).

movements.heading: Allemanda
movements.summary: A moderate dance in four, serious in tone: a winding line of quick notes, with a few chords to anchor it. Two halves, each played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The winding line
mainIdeas.description: even, steady notes that circle round and climb, anchored now and then by a chord.

stops.hear: A steady, winding line in the minor, with a chord here and there
The opening returns
The line sets off from a new note, moving through other keys
The second half again

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The line comes to rest on a low D

notice: Listen for the few chords. They mark the main points of the phrase, like posts along a path.

movements.heading: Corrente
movements.summary: A quicker dance in three, with a bouncing, dotted rhythm and runs of three quick notes that leap across the strings.

mainIdeas.name: The bounce
mainIdeas.description: long-short pairs of notes, then quick groups of three, so that the rhythm keeps changing gear.

stops.hear: A springy, quick line in three
The opening again
The music moves away from D minor
The second half again

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A firm close on D

notice: Notice how the violin jumps between a low note and a high one in quick succession, as if two players were taking turns.

movements.heading: Sarabanda
movements.summary: A slow dance in three, almost all in chords. The violin plays three or four notes together, so the music sounds full and grave, with the weight falling on the second beat of the bar.

mainIdeas.name: The chords
mainIdeas.description: rich, slow chords with a melody on top, played by bowing across several strings.

stops.hear: Slow, heavy chords, each one leaning on the middle beat
stops.happening: The first half of the [[sarabande|sarabande]], played with [[double-stop|double stop]]s and three- and four-note chords

stops.hear: The opening phrase again
A longer second half, rising higher and moving through new keys
The second half again

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A final chord on D

notice: Listen to how the violinist spreads each big chord: the lower notes sound a moment before the top one.

movements.heading: Giga
movements.summary: A fast jig in groups of three, a stream of notes that barely stops. It is the last of the dances, and the most brilliant.

mainIdeas.name: The stream
mainIdeas.description: quick notes in threes, racing up and down, with the lowest notes suggesting a bass line.

stops.hear: A rapid, unbroken run of notes in threes
The run starts again
The music turns to new keys and the leaps grow wider
The second half again

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The run settles on D

notice: Try to follow only the lowest notes. They form a slow bass line hidden inside the fast stream.

movements.heading: Ciaccona
movements.key: D minor – D major – D minor
movements.summary: A [[chaconne|chaconne]]: a short phrase of four bars and its harmonies, repeated more than sixty times while everything above it changes. The violin begins with heavy chords, dissolves them into running notes and broken chords, turns to the major for a long, calmer middle section, and then returns to the minor and to the chords of the opening.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: slow, solemn chords in a four-bar phrase, with the weight on the second beat, like a [[sarabande|sarabande]].

mainIdeas.name: The variations
mainIdeas.description: the same harmonies dressed in quicker and quicker notes, runs, leaps and broken chords.

mainIdeas.name: The major section
mainIdeas.description: a quieter, warmer world in D major, in the middle of the piece.

stops.hear: Slow, weighty chords, each phrase four bars long, the stress on the second beat
The chords loosen into a flowing line; the same harmonies sound underneath
Faster notes: runs and leaps that cover the whole violin
Rapid broken chords ripple across all four strings
stops.happening: Bach writes only the chords and marks the passage *arpeggio*; the player chooses the pattern of notes. See [[arpeggio|arpeggio]]

stops.hear: Chords again, slower and darker
stops.happening: The first, minor part draws to a close

stops.hear: The music turns to the major: soft, warm, hymn-like chords
stops.happening: The middle section, in D major

stops.hear: The major music grows fuller and stronger, with ringing chords
An abrupt return to the minor and to heavier chords
stops.happening: The last section, back in D minor

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The opening chords come back almost unchanged
stops.happening: The theme returns; the work ends on D

notice: Hold on to the four-bar phrase. Whatever the violin plays, a new pattern starts every four bars, and the same harmonies keep coming back.
Listen for the moment the music turns to D major, roughly halfway. Many listeners hear it as a sudden light.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Milstein recorded all six sonatas and partitas for Deutsche Grammophon in Conway Hall, London, in 1973, when he was in his late sixties; the set was released in 1975 and won a Grammy Award. It was his second recording of the set. He takes every repeat in the dances, which is why they last about four minutes each.

threads.title: One instrument, many voices
threads.body: In every movement the violin suggests more than one part: a bass under the melody in the dances, three and four voices at once in the Sarabanda and the Chaconne.

threads.title: Dances, then something larger
threads.body: The four dances follow the usual order of a suite. The Chaconne, also a dance in origin, grows into a piece as long as the other four together.

threads.title: D minor and its light
threads.body: Every movement is in D minor, and the dances only pass through other keys on the way. The turn to D major in the middle of the Chaconne, more than twenty minutes in, is the first time the music settles in the major.
